title: Singapore Airlines Puts Fresh Air India Funding Under Scrutiny as Losses Near $3 Billion
excerpt: The carrier's 25.1% stake has dragged SIA's profits down 57%, and analysts say more capital injections are unavoidable as Air India's turnaround proves costlier than expected.
body:
• Air India posted a net loss of approximately $3 billion (₹28,400 crore) in FY26 — nearly three times its FY25 loss — driven by Pakistan airspace closures, the Iran war, rupee depreciation and aftermath of the June 2025 crash.
  • Singapore Airlines' net profit fell 57% in FY26, with Air India losses largely responsible. SIA invested an additional $891 million into Air India during the year.
  • SIA has seconded two senior executives — Captain Basil Kwauk as COO and Jeremy Yew as head of engineering — to Air India, signalling deeper operational involvement.
  • Air India cut 27% of its international flights (nearly 150 weekly services) between June and August 2026 to stem losses, directly affecting millions of diaspora travellers.

Singapore Airlines is facing mounting pressure over its 25.1% stake in Air India as the Indian carrier's losses balloon to roughly $3 billion for the financial year ending March 2026 — nearly three times what it lost the previous year — forcing the Southeast Asian airline to weigh how much more capital it is willing to commit to one of aviation's most ambitious turnaround projects.

SIA's own net profit plunged 57% in FY26, with Air India's weak performance the primary drag. The Singaporean carrier invested an additional S$1.13 billion ($891 million) into Air India during the year, according to its annual report. CEO Goh Choon Phong has acknowledged the partnership will be a "long game" with "no shortcuts," but declined to comment on the scale of any future capital injections.

A Perfect Storm of Setbacks

Air India's losses stem from a cascade of external shocks that have compounded internal challenges. Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian carriers in April 2025, forcing longer and more expensive routing for flights to the Middle East and Europe. Weeks later, an Air India Boeing 787 crashed after takeoff from Ahmedabad, killing 260 people and triggering heightened regulatory scrutiny that forced the airline to scale back international operations.

"Aviation analyst Brendan Sobie told CNBC that SIA "will definitely have to put in more money."

The Iran conflict, which escalated from late February 2026, brought fresh airspace restrictions, route disruptions and a surge in jet fuel prices that nearly doubled between February and May. Air India's revenue totalled $8.27 billion in FY26, but costs — denominated largely in US dollars against a weakening rupee — swallowed the gains and then some.

"It is going to be a long game. There will be no shortcuts."

— Goh Choon Phong, CEO, Singapore Airlines

Deeper Involvement, Not Less

Rather than pulling back, Singapore Airlines has deepened its operational involvement. The airline seconded Captain Basil Kwauk as chief operations officer and Jeremy Yew as head of engineering and maintenance at Air India — key roles that place SIA veterans at the heart of the turnaround effort across flight operations, safety and fleet management.

Tata Sons, which holds the remaining 74.9% stake, is focusing on commercial, human resources, finance and IT functions. SIA CEO Goh and Tata Group Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran met in Mumbai to discuss a funding roadmap and the search for a new CEO after Campbell Wilson resigned earlier this year.

Analysts, however, say more cash will inevitably be needed. "Given the magnitude of losses and continued operating pressure, the capital required in this round is likely to be meaningfully higher than initially expected," DBS Group Research analyst Jason Sum wrote. Aviation analyst Brendan Sobie told CNBC that SIA "will definitely have to put in more money. There's no question about that."

What It Means for Indian Travellers

Air India's financial crisis has direct consequences for the diaspora. The airline cancelled 27% of its international flights — nearly 150 weekly services — between June and August 2026 to control costs. Routes connecting India with the Middle East, Europe and North America have been cut or reduced, disrupting travel plans for millions of NRIs during the peak summer travel season.

The airline's net promoter score has improved by 50 points under the transformation programme, according to Goh, reflecting genuine progress in training, in-flight services and lounge quality. But for passengers facing cancelled flights and limited alternatives on routes like Delhi-London or Mumbai-Dubai, the financial restructuring behind the scenes translates to fewer seats and higher fares.

The Long View

India is investing heavily in airport infrastructure, and air travel demand is growing faster than almost anywhere in the world. NUS professor Sumit Agarwal noted that despite the short-term pain, "it's a good bet to be in that market. The demand is there." Air India has ordered more than 470 new aircraft, though delivery delays have strained timelines. Whether SIA's patience — and capital — holds long enough for the turnaround to take hold will determine the future of India's flag carrier and the travel options available to the diaspora for years to come.
